name: Bantu
line: Go slowly, add a little each day, keep the common ground, speak in proverbs and tell a story at night.

quote.text: Little by little fills the measure.

quotes.text: One hand does not raise a child.
One head cannot carry a roof.
quotes.source: Mutu umodzi susenza denga. Said in Malawi and Zambia

quotes.text: Teeth that stand together are the ones that bite the meat.
quotes.source: Agali awamu ge galuma ennyama. Said in Uganda
Gũtirĩ mũthenya ũkĩaga ta ũngĩ. Said in Kenya

quotes.text: A person is a person through other people.
quotes.source: Motho ke motho ka batho. The same saying is found across the Bantu languages

words.usage: The plural of a word for person, formed with the prefix ba-. In 1862 a German linguist chose it as the name for the whole family of languages that share it.
The singular: mu- for one human being, ba- for several. Umuntu in Zulu, mtu in Swahili, munhu in Shona, motho in Sotho.
What is left when the prefix is taken off. Philosophers such as Alexis Kagame built an account of Bantu thought on the classes of things this root can form.
The quality of being a true person. The same word as ubuntu in Zulu, unhu in Shona and umunthu in Chewa.
Respect, courtesy and compassion. It is named as a national principle of Botswana.
Said to anyone arriving, and in answer to a knock. Karibu chakula means come and eat.
A greeting asks for news: of the morning, of home, of work, of the children. The answer is nzuri, good, before anything else is said.
Said by a younger person to an older one. The elder answers marahaba.
Asante sana is thank you very much.

words.meaning: I am sorry for your trouble
words.usage: Said to anyone who is tired, hurt, bereaved or simply carrying something heavy. Said twice, pole pole, it means slowly.
The greeting of both banks of the Congo river. It means goodness.
A title of respect for an older man, and for founding leaders.
The title by which Julius Nyerere, a schoolteacher who became president, was always known.
The spirits of the family’s dead, who guard their descendants. Mizimu in Swahili and badimo in Tswana come from the same root.

words.language: Chewa, Yao and many East African languages
words.usage: The creator, distant and above all spirits. Other Bantu languages say Nzambi, Mwari, Leza or Modimo.

words.meaning: Drum; dance; a gathering to heal
words.usage: One word across half a continent for the drum, the music and dance made with it, and the rites of healing it serves.
Metal keys on a wooden board, played inside a gourd. Its music calls the ancestors at Shona ceremonies.
The teller calls hadithi, hadithi, and the listeners answer hadithi njoo, story, come.
The compressed wisdom of the elders. A case is argued, and a child corrected, with a proverb.
A work call of dock labourers that Jomo Kenyatta made the motto of Kenya. It now means a community fundraising.
Living and working together as one extended family. Nyerere made it the name of Tanzania’s village socialism.

words.meaning: Coming together for a common purpose
words.usage: Shared labour for the community. In Rwanda the last Saturday morning of each month is given to it by law.
A meeting place by the chief’s cattle enclosure where any adult may speak and matters are settled by consensus. It is also the customary court.
An open shelter at the centre of a Kongo village where people gather around a fire to hear disputes, teach the young and receive strangers.
The family’s cultivated land. Most Bantu-speaking peoples have been farmers for three thousand years.
A word that has barely changed in four thousand years: inkomo in Zulu, mombe in Shona, kgomo in Tswana.
The staple from Kenya to the Cape under many names: sadza, nsima, pap, posho. Eaten with the hand from a common dish.
A cry of the independence movements, it is dawn. Zambia and Malawi named their money after it.
The word for independence across East Africa. The highest point of Kilimanjaro bears the name.
From dzimba dza mabwe. The name of the great walled capital and, since 1980, of the country.

practices.name: Pole pole: one thing slowly
practices.instructions: Take the first task of your day and do it at half your usual speed. Make the tea, wash, sweep, write the first message, walk to the bus, without rushing and without doing anything else at once. Give it your whole attention until it is properly finished. If someone speaks to you, stop and answer them fully before you go on. Notice what the hurry was for.
practices.why: The Swahili proverb says that hurry, hurry has no blessing, and pole pole, slowly, is advice heard every day from the coast to the lakes. Time in village life is measured by tasks and by people. Greeting a neighbour properly comes before the business one came for.
variations: Walk somewhere today without checking the time.
Let a conversation run until it is finished.
Say pole to someone who is tired or struggling.

practices.name: Little by little
practices.instructions: Choose one thing that can only be done over a long time: a language, a debt, a skill, a field, a book, a friendship. Give it fifteen minutes today, and only fifteen. Do a small, definite piece and stop. Mark the day on a calendar. Tomorrow add the next piece. Do not try to make up for lost days, and do not skip one because the piece seems too small to matter.
practices.why: Haba na haba hujaza kibaba: little by little fills the measure. The proverb comes from a world of farmers who cleared forest with hoes and built granaries a basket at a time. Village savings circles, in which each member puts in a small sum every week, work on the same principle.
variations: Put aside one coin a day.
Learn three words a day of a Bantu language.
Start a savings circle with friends.

practices.name: Keep the common ground
practices.instructions: Spend twenty minutes on a place that belongs to everyone and so to no one: the pavement outside your door, a stairwell, a path, a park, a bus shelter. Sweep it, clear the litter, unblock the drain, cut back what is overgrown. Ask a neighbour to join you. Afterwards stand for a minute and talk with whoever is there about what else the place needs.
practices.why: In Rwanda the last Saturday morning of every month is umuganda. Shops close, traffic stops and each neighbourhood turns out to clean streets, dig ditches and build houses for those in need, and then holds a meeting. Kenyans call such joint effort harambee, and Tswana speakers letsema.
variations: Fix a day each month for your street to do this together.
Help build or repair something for a neighbour who cannot.
Go to a local public meeting.

practices.name: Carry a proverb
practices.instructions: Learn one proverb today, from this Onda or from your own grandparents. Say it aloud until you have it by heart. Then think of one situation in your life that it fits, and one that it does not. Before the day ends, use it in conversation in place of giving advice or winning an argument. Write it in your journal with the date.
practices.why: In Bantu-speaking societies a proverb is the proper way to make a point. Elders settle disputes with them, parents correct children with them, and a speaker who uses them well is thought wise. They put a hard truth indirectly, so that no one is shamed. Collections in Swahili, Shona, Kikuyu and Zulu run to thousands.
variations: Ask an older relative for a saying from their childhood.
Answer a question today with a proverb and nothing more.
Collect one proverb a day for the month.

practices.name: Tell a story with a chorus
practices.instructions: After the evening meal, tell a story aloud to whoever is in the house. Begin with a call that your listeners must answer, such as story, story, and wait for story, come. Tell a tale you were told, or what happened today as if it were a tale. Give it a short line or a song that comes round several times, for everyone to join in. End with what the story is for.
practices.why: Before writing, everything was carried in spoken word, and the evening fire was the school. Folktales of the clever hare and the greedy hyena are told from Cameroon to the Cape, with a set opening exchange and with songs that the audience sings. The drum, the ngoma, turns the same gathering into dance.
variations: Tell a hare story to a child.
Clap a steady rhythm together and let people take turns over it.
Ask the oldest person present for a story.

tasks.name: Read a chapter of The River Between
Listen to mbira music
tasks.meta: Listen · Stella Chiweshe, or any recording of the Shona mbira

tasks.name: Look at a Luba memory board
tasks.meta: Art · a lukasa, read with the fingers

tasks.name: Play bao
tasks.meta: Games · the sowing game of the Swahili coast, or any mancala

tasks.name: Journal: what did you add to today, little by little?
Can one head carry a roof?
Greet an older person first, and ask for their news
Welcome someone in and feed them
Eat from a shared dish tonight

rules.why: Hurry has no blessing. Finish one thing and greet people properly.
Small, steady work fills the measure.
One head cannot carry a roof. Call others, and come when called.

rules.text: Honour your elders and your dead
rules.why: They went ahead of you. Greet them first and remember their names.
Say come near, and share what is in the pot.
Put hard things in a proverb or a story, so that no one is shamed.

read.title: The River Between
read.creator: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o
read.why: Two Kikuyu villages on facing ridges are divided by the coming of the missions. A short, clear novel by the writer who later chose to write only in his own language.

read.title: Nervous Conditions
read.creator: Tsitsi Dangarembga
read.why: A Shona girl in 1960s Rhodesia fights for the schooling her brother was given. Sharp on family, hunger and the price of an education.

read.title: Paradise
read.creator: Abdulrazak Gurnah
read.why: A boy is pawned to a merchant and travels with a caravan from the Swahili coast into the interior, on the eve of German rule.

read.title: Unbowed
read.creator: Wangari Maathai
read.why: The memoir of the Kikuyu scientist who founded the Green Belt Movement and planted tens of millions of trees.

read.title: Chaka
read.creator: Thomas Mofolo
read.why: A tragic novel of the Zulu king written in Sesotho. One of the first novels in an African language.

read.title: Facing Mount Kenya
read.creator: Jomo Kenyatta
read.why: An account of Kikuyu life by the man who would be Kenya’s first president, written as a student of anthropology in London.

watch.title: Lumumba
watch.creator: Raoul Peck
watch.why: The few months in 1960 and 1961 in which Patrice Lumumba led the Congo to independence and was destroyed.

watch.title: The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind
watch.creator: Chiwetel Ejiofor
watch.why: A true story from Malawi, largely in Chichewa. During a famine a schoolboy builds a windmill from scrap to pump water.

watch.title: Neria
watch.creator: Godwin Mawuru
watch.why: A widow in Zimbabwe fights her husband’s brother for her home and children. Written by Tsitsi Dangarembga.

watch.title: Félicité
watch.creator: Alain Gomis
watch.why: A singer in a Kinshasa bar searches the city for money to save her son. In Lingala, with the music of the Kasai Allstars.

listen.title: Francophonic
listen.creator: Franco and TPOK Jazz
listen.why: The giant of Congolese rumba, whose long guitar-led songs were heard across the whole continent.

listen.title: Ambuya?
listen.creator: Stella Chiweshe
listen.why: The mbira of the Shona, played by one of the first women to master an instrument long reserved for men.

listen.title: Pata Pata
listen.creator: Miriam Makeba
listen.why: Songs in Xhosa, Zulu and Swahili by the singer the world called Mama Africa.

listen.title: Zanzibar
listen.creator: Bi Kidude
listen.why: Taarab and the drum songs of the Swahili coast, from a singer who performed for some eighty years.

art.title: The Zimbabwe birds
art.creator: Carvers of Great Zimbabwe
art.why: Eight birds of prey in soapstone that stood on pillars in the royal enclosure. One is on the national flag.

art.title: Kuba cloth
art.creator: Kuba weavers and embroiderers, Congo
art.why: Men weave panels of raffia palm and women work them in cut pile with interlocking geometric designs, each with a name.

art.title: The lukasa
art.creator: Luba court historians, Congo
art.why: A hand-sized wooden board studded with beads and shells. A trained elder touches it to recall the history of kings.

art.title: Ndebele house painting
art.creator: Esther Mahlangu and the women of the Ndebele
art.why: Bold bands and blocks of colour outlined in black, painted freehand on the walls of homes.

eat.title: Ugali
eat.creator: Stiff maize or millet porridge
eat.why: Rolled into a ball with the right hand, dented with the thumb and used to scoop up relish.

eat.title: Greens
eat.creator: Sukuma wiki, fried with onion and tomato
eat.why: The name means push the week. The cheap dish that stretches a household’s money.

eat.title: Matoke
eat.creator: Steamed green bananas, mashed
eat.why: The staple of Buganda, cooked in banana leaves.

eat.title: Cassava leaves
eat.creator: Pondu, pounded and stewed with palm oil
eat.why: The everyday relish of the Congo basin.

eat.title: Pilau
eat.creator: Rice cooked in spiced broth
eat.why: The feast dish of the Swahili coast, where Africa met Arabia and India.

drink.title: Spiced tea
drink.creator: Chai with ginger, boiled with milk
drink.why: Sold from kettles on every street corner of East Africa.

drink.title: Palm wine
drink.creator: The sap of the raffia or oil palm
drink.why: Sweet in the morning and sour by evening. The drink of ceremony in the Congo basin.

drink.title: Banana beer
drink.creator: Brewed from ripe bananas and sorghum
drink.why: Shared through straws from one pot in Rwanda, Burundi and around the great lakes.

customs.title: Greeting an elder
customs.creator: Shikamoo and marahaba
customs.why: On the Swahili coast a younger person offers this greeting, and the elder returns a blessing.

customs.title: Washing hands and the common dish
customs.creator: Eating together
customs.why: Water is poured over each person’s hands, eldest first, and everyone eats from one dish with the right hand.

customs.title: Naming after grandparents
customs.creator: The Kikuyu pattern
customs.why: The first son is named for the father’s father and the first daughter for the father’s mother, and the next two for the mother’s parents. The grandparents live again in the children.

customs.title: The long handshake
customs.creator: Hands held while talking
customs.why: Friends may go on holding hands through a whole greeting. A hand to the right forearm adds respect.

games.title: Bao
games.creator: Board game · the Swahili coast
games.why: A sowing game on four rows of eight pits with sixty-four seeds. The most complex of all the mancala games, with recognised masters.

games.title: Omweso
games.creator: Board game · Uganda
games.why: The royal game of Buganda, played very fast on four rows of eight. Kings were once tested at it.

games.title: Nhodo
games.creator: Stone game · Zimbabwe
games.why: One stone is tossed up while others are swept in and out of a hole in the ground.

games.title: Morabaraba
games.creator: Board game · southern Africa
games.why: Each player has twelve tokens called cows and tries to form rows of three.

festivals.title: Kuomboka
festivals.creator: March or April, western Zambia
festivals.why: When the Zambezi floods, the Lozi king is rowed in a great black and white barge from the plain to higher ground, to the sound of royal drums.

festivals.title: Umuganura
festivals.creator: The first Friday of August, Rwanda
festivals.why: The festival of first fruits. The harvest is shared and the year’s work reviewed.

festivals.title: Sauti za Busara
festivals.creator: February, Zanzibar
festivals.why: Sounds of Wisdom. Four days of live music from across the continent inside the old fort of Stone Town.

festivals.title: World Kiswahili Language Day
festivals.creator: 7 July
festivals.why: Proclaimed by UNESCO in 2021, the first such day for an African language.

places.title: Great Zimbabwe
places.creator: Near Masvingo, Zimbabwe
places.why: The granite walls of a city of some eighteen thousand people that flourished from the eleventh to the fifteenth century. The outer wall of the Great Enclosure is eleven metres high and built without mortar.

places.title: Kilwa Kisiwani
places.creator: The south coast of Tanzania
places.why: The ruins of the richest Swahili city of the fourteenth century, with its great mosque and palace.

places.title: Lamu Old Town
places.creator: The north coast of Kenya
places.why: The oldest continuously lived-in Swahili town, a maze of coral stone houses with carved doors and no cars.

places.title: Mbanza Kongo
places.creator: Northern Angola
places.why: The capital of the Kingdom of Kongo, on a plateau where its kings were crowned and buried.

places.title: The Kasubi Tombs
places.creator: Kampala, Uganda
places.why: The burial place of four kings of Buganda, under a vast thatched dome that was rebuilt after a fire in 2010.

places.title: Mapungubwe
places.creator: Limpopo, South Africa
places.why: The hill where the rulers of southern Africa’s first kingdom lived about 1220. A small rhinoceros of gold foil was found in a grave here.

ethics.title: Utu
ethics.text: Be a real person: humane, generous, considerate.
ethics.practice: Do something kind for a stranger.

ethics.title: Respect for elders
ethics.text: Age is experience. Greet first and listen.
ethics.practice: Ask an older person for advice and take it.

ethics.title: Hospitality
ethics.text: A guest is a blessing. There is always enough for one more.

ethics.title: Solidarity
ethics.practice: Turn up for someone else’s task.

ethics.title: Patience
ethics.practice: Do not hurry one thing today.

ethics.title: Indirection
ethics.practice: Say something difficult through a story.

philosophy.title: I am because we are
philosophy.text: John Mbiti summed up the view in one line: I am because we are, and since we are, therefore I am.
philosophy.practice: Which we are you because of?

philosophy.title: Being as force
philosophy.text: Some thinkers describe a Bantu view of being as living force that can be strengthened or weakened by how one lives with others. Other African philosophers reject so general a claim.
philosophy.practice: What strengthens life in you, and what weakens it?

philosophy.title: The living, the dead and the unborn
philosophy.text: A family includes those who have gone and those still to come.
philosophy.practice: What do you owe to people you will never meet?

philosophy.title: Consensus
philosophy.text: At the kgotla people talk until they agree. A decision that divides the community is not a decision.
philosophy.practice: Where do you settle for winning a vote?

philosophy.title: Little by little
philosophy.text: Great things are the sum of small ones done faithfully.
philosophy.practice: What are you trying to do all at once?

philosophy.title: The wisdom of the indirect
philosophy.text: A proverb lets the hearer reach the conclusion themselves.
philosophy.practice: What do you say too bluntly?

philosophy.title: Familyhood
philosophy.text: Nyerere held that a nation should work as an extended family, in which no one is rich while another goes hungry.
philosophy.practice: How far does your family extend?

philosophy.title: Many peoples, one root
philosophy.text: Hundreds of nations share related words and none of them is the same.
philosophy.practice: What do you share with people you think of as foreign?

intro: Bantu is the name of a family of languages, not of a people. It takes in some five hundred related languages spoken across the southern half of Africa by about 350 million people, among them Swahili, Zulu, Xhosa, Shona, Kikuyu, Ganda, Kinyarwanda, Lingala, Kongo, Bemba, Chewa, Sotho and Tswana. The name was chosen in 1862 by the linguist Wilhelm Bleek, who noticed that in language after language the word for people was some form of ba-ntu. The speakers of these languages belong to hundreds of distinct nations with their own histories, and none has ever called itself Bantu.

The languages are alike because they descend from one ancestor, spoken about five thousand years ago in the borderland of what are now Nigeria and Cameroon. From there, over some three thousand years, farming communities who made pottery and later worked iron spread east and south through the rainforest and around it, reaching the great lakes of East Africa about three thousand years ago and the far south-east of the continent by about AD 300. They mixed with and largely absorbed the hunters and herders who lived there before them. It was one of the great migrations of human history, and it was slow: a matter of villages moving a few kilometres in a generation.

The shared inheritance shows in grammar and vocabulary. Bantu languages sort all nouns into classes marked by prefixes, so that one root gives the words for a person, people, a language, a country and a quality. Words for cattle, drum, ancestor and chief are recognisably the same across thousands of kilometres. With the words go habits of life that are widely shared, though never uniform: farming with the hoe, the keeping of cattle in the east and south, respect for elders, the continuing presence of the ancestors, decisions reached in open assembly, and a rich art of proverb, story, song and drum.

Speakers of Bantu languages built many states. On the east coast, from about the eighth century, the Swahili towns traded gold and ivory across the Indian Ocean. Inland, the rulers of Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe raised palaces of stone. The Kingdom of Kongo exchanged ambassadors with Portugal and the Pope. Luba, Lunda, Buganda, Rwanda, the Zulu and the Sotho all formed powerful kingdoms.

From the sixteenth century the Atlantic slave trade carried off millions of people from the Congo and Angola, more than from any other part of Africa, and with them the words and rhythms that shaped the music and religion of Brazil, Cuba and the American South. Colonial conquest followed in the 1880s, with particular horror in the Congo. In South Africa the apartheid state used the word Bantu as its official label for Black people, and it remains offensive there when applied to persons.
Independence came between 1960 and 1994. Swahili, with perhaps two hundred million speakers, is now a working language of the African Union.
This Onda takes its practices from habits found widely among these peoples, and names the language each word comes from.
guide.origin: From Cameroon across the Congo basin to Kenya and south to the Cape
guide.era: The first Bantu speakers lived about five thousand years ago. Some 350 million people speak a Bantu language today

figures.name: Afonso I of Kongo
figures.bio: Mvemba a Nzinga. A Christian king who wrote some two dozen surviving letters to the kings of Portugal, asking for teachers and doctors and protesting at the seizure of his people as slaves.

figures.name: Nzinga Mbande
figures.bio: Queen of Ndongo and Matamba in what is now Angola. Diplomat and commander, she resisted the Portuguese for forty years.

figures.name: Kimpa Vita
figures.bio: A young Kongo noblewoman who led a movement to reunite the kingdom and taught that Jesus and the saints were Kongolese. She was burned as a heretic.

figures.name: Moshoeshoe I
figures.bio: Founder of the Basotho nation. From his mountain fortress he gathered refugees of the wars and kept his kingdom by diplomacy as much as by arms.

figures.name: Nehanda Nyakasikana
figures.bio: A Shona spirit medium who inspired the rising of 1896 against the British South Africa Company and was hanged. She is honoured as the grandmother of Zimbabwe.

figures.name: Khama III
figures.bio: King of the Bangwato, who travelled to London in 1895 and kept his country out of the hands of Cecil Rhodes.

figures.name: Alexis Kagame
figures.bio: Rwandan priest, poet and historian who analysed the grammar of his language to set out a Bantu philosophy of being.

figures.name: Nelson Mandela
figures.bio: A Xhosa of the Thembu royal house, lawyer, prisoner for twenty-seven years and first president of a democratic South Africa.

figures.name: Julius Nyerere
figures.bio: Teacher and first president of Tanzania. He made Swahili the language of the nation and translated Shakespeare into it.

figures.name: Patrice Lumumba
figures.bio: First prime minister of the independent Congo, overthrown and murdered within seven months.

figures.name: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o
figures.bio: Kenyan novelist who was imprisoned for a play in Kikuyu and from then on wrote his fiction in that language.

figures.name: Wangari Maathai
figures.bio: Kenyan biologist and founder of the Green Belt Movement. The first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

history.detail: The ancestral Bantu language is spoken by farmers of yams and oil palms in the grasslands of western Cameroon.
Communities spread along the rivers and the coast into the Congo basin and reach the great lakes.
Smelting furnaces are in use around Lake Victoria. Iron hoes and axes speed the clearing of land.
Farmers who speak Bantu languages are settled south of the Limpopo.
Trading towns grow up from Somalia to Mozambique. Their people become Muslim, build in coral stone and speak a Bantu language rich in Arabic words.
Kingdoms on the plateau grow rich on gold and ivory sold to the coast. Great Zimbabwe is at its height in the fourteenth century.
A state forms south of the Congo river. Portuguese ships arrive in 1483, and the king is baptised in 1491.
More than five million people are shipped from the ports of Kongo and Angola to the Americas.
Luba, Lunda, Buganda and Rwanda are at their strongest. Caravans from Zanzibar bring guns and take ivory and slaves.
The Berlin conference divides the continent. In the Congo Free State of King Leopold II, forced rubber collection kills millions.
German forces in South West Africa drive the Herero into the desert. Most of the nation dies.
South Africa classifies Black people as Bantu, gives them an inferior Bantu education and assigns them to ten homelands.
The Congo in 1960, Tanganyika in 1961, Kenya in 1963, Zambia and Malawi in 1964, Angola and Mozambique in 1975, Zimbabwe in 1980, Namibia in 1990 and a free South Africa in 1994.
UNESCO proclaims a world day for the language, and the African Union adopts it as a working language.

concepts.detail: Bantu languages are as closely related as the Romance or Germanic languages. A Swahili speaker can recognise many words of Zulu.
Every noun belongs to a class with its own prefix, and adjectives and verbs agree with it. Mu-ntu is a person, ba-ntu people, ki-ntu a thing, bu-ntu humanity.
Not a conquest or a single journey. Small groups budded off and moved on over a hundred generations, taking crops, pottery and language with them.
A child is brought into humanity by others, through naming, teaching and initiation, and adults keep it by how they behave.
Those who have died and are still remembered by name remain close to the family and are consulted and honoured.
Villages and kingdoms alike were run through councils of senior men, and sometimes women, who deliberated in public.
Proverbs, riddles, folktales, praise poems, epics and songs carried law, history and morals without writing.

concepts.text: Drum, dance and healing as one.
concepts.detail: Illness and misfortune are treated in gatherings of music and movement that restore a person to their community.

concepts.text: A Bantu language of the world.
concepts.detail: Born of African and Indian Ocean trade, it is now a first or second language from Somalia to the Congo.

facts.text: Swahili has no native speakers in most of the countries where it is spoken. It is a second language for the great majority of its users.
The word safari is Swahili, from an Arabic word for a journey.
The banjo, the samba, the conga and the word zombie all trace back to the peoples of Kongo and Angola.
The walls of Great Zimbabwe contain about a million granite blocks, laid without mortar.
Linguists have reconstructed several thousand words of the ancestral Bantu language, including words for canoe, goat, pot and drum.
Some Bantu languages of the south, such as Zulu and Xhosa, took their click sounds from the Khoisan peoples they met.

sensitivity.note: Bantu is a family of languages spoken by hundreds of different peoples, and there is no single Bantu culture. This Onda gathers habits that are widely shared, names the language of every word and proverb, and should be reviewed by speakers of those languages.
requiredCaveats: In South Africa the word Bantu was the apartheid state’s label for Black people and is offensive when applied to persons. Here it is used only in its linguistic sense.
Customs differ greatly between, say, the Swahili coast, the Congo forest and the southern grasslands. Nothing said here is true of every people.
The idea of a single Bantu philosophy was first set out by a Belgian missionary in 1945 and has been strongly criticised by African philosophers.
Rites of initiation, healing and the ancestors belong to particular communities and are not practices for outsiders.
